source.title: From "Weak" Signals to Strong Models: Preference Delta Aggregation with LoRA Merging
source.authors: Qi Sun; Siyue Zhang; Yu-Lin Chen; Yuxiang Xue; Ru Peng; Chen Zhao

page_placements.theme: Multiple weak supervisors: assignment, weighting, boosting, merging and diversity

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present, including appendices and checklist; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether preference tuning of a stronger student on relative quality signals from weaker model pairs improves performance, and compares aggregation strategies. It uses pairwise preference optimization and LoRA merging rather than the original Burns et al. setup, and does not calculate PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports average benchmark scores for student baselines, single-delta tuning, and multi-delta methods; those aggregate scores are recorded below. It also reports per-benchmark scores that are not separately extracted here. The case studies and behavior-analysis percentages concern specific reasoning behaviors rather than the versions' main performance measure. The ZeroSearch failure and SFT control are included because they directly bear on whether weak signals improve the student.
record.test_reason: A strong 8B student is trained on supervision from weaker models: preference pairs from a weak and a weaker model, plus an SFT control on the weak model's outputs alone. It is scored against its own baseline and, via Table 4, against the supervisors. This bears on V1, V2 and V3 by a different method. No PGR is computed and there is no ground-truth strong ceiling. Unlike Burns et al., the untuned student already outperforms every supervisor, so beating the supervisor is not by itself evidence of weak-to-strong generalization.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Authors conclude that weak-weaker preference deltas improve stronger students on reasoning and agentic search, and that LoRA merging (especially GAM) aggregates multiple deltas beyond any single one, while sequential and joint training do not. Deltas are not universally beneficial (ZeroSearch failure), and gains need directionally diverse pairs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pairwise preference data from weak-weaker model pairs and DPO/ORPO tuning, then aggregates independently trained LoRA adapters; it does not use Burns et al.'s original intervention or report PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by weak-weaker pair and task. Agentic search uses ORPO rather than DPO to retain formatting; GAM results are reported for different delta counts. The paper says aggregating behaviorally homogeneous pairs yields only marginal improvement and reports a ZeroSearch-pair failure.

fits_no_version.finding: Different weak pairs induce distinct search-behaviour specialisations (e.g. Search-R1 delta verification 5.3% vs Qwen3 delta 75.9%). Merging restores a balance (61.2% verification, 56.7% adaptive search).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak supervisors transmit supervisor-specific behavioural biases that combining supervisors can offset

record.code_released: Not released at submission; authors say code and data will be released after the review period. Repository path stated as AlbertQiSun/Preference-Delta-Aggregation.
record.problems: No error bars or statistical significance tests are reported. PGR is not calculated. The experiments cover a limited set of student models and weak-weaker pairs; the authors note the need to study broader collections. Some comparisons rely on aggregate suite averages, and matched weak-supervisor scores are not supplied for every reported aggregate.
record.rows_left_out: Per-benchmark values from Tables 1 and 2, additional individual merging-method results for some Tülu3-8B conditions, the full SFT per-benchmark breakdown, and the 500-sample behavior-analysis rates in Table 3 are not separately extracted; the aggregate scores and claim-relevant controls/failure result are prioritized. Tables 1, 2, 3 and 16; Section 6.1.

untested.parts: PGR against a ground-truth-trained strong ceiling; a setting where the student starts below the supervisor.
Auxiliary confidence loss; PGR as the outcome measure.
Student-size sweep (only 8B students); supervisor-size sweep beyond the fixed pairs; chess and reward modelling; predictors such as error similarity.
Not tested: exploitation of what the supervisor cannot check, distribution shift, error similarity.
Not tested; the Appendix C analysis concerns LoRA merging noise, not student-beats-supervisor conditions.

missing.what: Absolute supervisor scores for all weak and weaker models, needed to compare tuned students with their supervisors for V1. The rows instead use the student's own baseline.
Tülu3-8B multi-delta results for averaging, KnOTS, TIES and GAM 2Δ on reasoning (73.7, 75.2, 75.0, 75.4, 75.9) and on search (55.7, 55.5, 54.3, 55.7, 56.0, 53.7, 55.9).

record.verdict_notes: The design departs from Burns et al.: students outperform supervisors before training, and there is no ground-truth ceiling, so PGR cannot be computed. The SFT control (Appendix I) is the closest analogue to weak-label fine-tuning. For Tülu3-8B it pulls the student below the supervisor on the multi-hop average, by my computation from Tables 4 and 16. The reader's Qwen3-8B agentic multi-delta averages were partly taken from the Tülu columns of garbled Table 2; the corrections above are confirmed by the text (57.4 for TIES 4Δ, 3.2 and 0.6 point gaps). No error bars are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports student and tuned-student performance and states that supervisors underperform students, but does not calculate PGR or report matched weak-supervisor scores in the same aggregate evaluation for every condition.

Compares multi-delta aggregation and merging approaches with single-delta and training-based approaches. Does not test auxiliary confidence loss or the specific ensembling/loss variants named in the claim.

Tests reasoning and agentic-search tasks, Qwen3-8B and Tülu3-8B students, and several weak-weaker pairs. Does not systematically sweep student or supervisor sizes or test whether error similarity predicts PGR.
Does not test supervisor-uncheckable exploitation, distribution shift, or whether gains shrink when weak and strong models make similar errors.
The appendix gives an idealized analysis of GAM merging, not conditions requiring a student to beat its supervisor.
